endorsements.quote: Algorithms must be validated—not only for performance, fairness, and reliability, but also for their real‐world impact on clinician and patient satisfaction, healthcare costs, patient access, and outcomes.
Both clinicians and patients need training in responsible AI use, with the understanding that to err is human, and AI.
To truly support care, AI must be thoughtfully integrated into workflows, with user‐friendly interfaces and clear professional guidelines.

unlisted_practices: Validate AI tools in condition-specific populations rather than only broad cohorts.
Embed clinical AI risk predictions in structured decision-support pathways that trigger follow-up actions.
Pair AI predictions with confidence intervals so clinicians can apply professional judgment.
Use explainable AI to expose the factors driving decisions and enable scrutiny of fairness and bias.
Rigorously validate patient-facing AI suggestions to ensure they are appropriate for the patient.
Have patient-facing self-help AI platforms provide automated prompts advising patients when to contact a clinician.
Report AI red flags as would be done with a human clinician.
Use large language models as the interface while explainable machine learning models generate the actual recommendations.
Avoid relying on general-purpose large language models for transcribing and summarizing conversations in non-English or mixed languages without domain and language adaptation.
Treat any AI-generated input capable of influencing patient behavior as an intervention.

screen.reason: Commentary discussing the perceptions, risks, governance, and deployment practices (validation, workflow integration, maintaining human oversight) of AI in healthcare, specifically eating disorders.
